title: Hooks are a second, narrower extension mechanism: operator-configured commands with a closed set of answers
A hook source is trusted through configuration, and a hook that could not answer denies at the two gating points
The Claude Code mods bridge and its band are not built
Auto review is kept as a policy listener whose request and verdict are logged, and whose removal tightens
Webhook rules are configuration, the ingress is its own listener, and an unattended session cannot be widened
Ralph is a Go loop on the subagent seam; it is neither a workflow nor a goal
The OAR provider is a Runner on the subagent seam, and its selector is the shared delegation tool
One terminal service: six tools on it, control passes to the person and does not come back, and reading the person's terminals is opt-in
A hook command runs under one protocol, for a bounded time, and leaves a record
Existing Claude Code and Codex hook files fire at nine points and can only restrict or annotate
An auto permission choice has a model review every tool call, on the record
A verified outside event starts an ordinary session by a configured rule, once
A signed GitHub delivery is accepted on a listener that serves nothing else
A person can ask for a bounded loop of fresh agents on one objective
A task can be delegated to an OAR runtime the operator installed, and nothing is left running
The model has six tools for terminals a person can watch and take over, and can read the person's terminals when allowed
Hook outcome decoder table with a fuzz target, order-free merge, identical commands run once, paired and bounded log records
A hook's process tree is stopped on timeout and cancel; a hook that could not answer denies at the gating points; the environment is scrubbed and holds no call token
Through a fake pipeline a hook denies, asks and blocks, never overrides a downstream denial, and never changes logged arguments
Session-start context is in the first request; a rejected prompt blocks the turn; forced continuations are capped; continue false ends the turn with cause extension
Both dialect files load with their matcher rules and aliases; unsupported entries are listed; an untrusted or changed project file runs nothing; an edited file is re-read
Reviewer verdict table, ask and never paths, nested calls, authority by source, a request rebuildable from the log, and unload that tightens
Webhook rule conditions, labelled payload block, preset allow-list, delivery record states, duplicate suppression, bounds, rollback, and no answerer
GitHub ingress status table in order, no parsing before verification, secret rotation, and separation of the ingress and UI listeners
Ralph rounds, handoff rules, every bound, one retry, cancellation that waits for the child, and denial outside a human turn or for a delegated agent
The OAR provider registers on the subagent seam with its capabilities and requirements, fails one delegation when Node is missing, and settles with a confinement record
Terminal tools pass the caller as owner, bound results, translate named keys, respect person control, and the user-terminal tools are off by default and read-only
Real hook scripts gate a real model's tool calls on three systems
A real model is reviewed in auto, attended and unattended, and completes a two-round ralph run
A real GitHub delivery starts one unattended session
Delegation to one real installed runtime through OAR starts, answers, cancels and leaves no process
A person watches an agent terminal in a real browser and takes it over

reason: The auto permission preset is kept as one default-off component, x/autoreview: a tools.Decide listener that asks the session's own model for a verdict before every tool body. Two things change: the reviewer request and its verdict are committed session events, and unloading the component moves live auto sessions to read-only instead of full access.

A mod is a JavaScript module whose register function must run inside the host process with the $ interface as live objects (README lines 28 and 99). The Go host loads no code and embeds no interpreter, and the plugin protocol offers no interception. Guarding tools, adding context and reacting to a stop are covered by hooks; tools and commands by a plugin process.

The package only draws the band a mod renders above the prompt and sends button presses back to mod code. With the mods bridge not built there is nothing to draw, and a plugin process cannot add UI in the Go design.

The shared engine is kept in Go form inside x/hooks: the exit-code and JSON outcome decoder, the two matcher modes, the most-restrictive merge and the paired hook/invoked and hook/result events. The runner uses area A09's process starter, runs matched hooks concurrently, and treats a hook that could not answer as a denial at the two gating points.

The Claude Code bridge is no longer a package of its own: it is the claude-code dialect of the one x/hooks component (a file reader, payload shapes and matcher rule), and its seven points are listeners on agent.Created, agent.PreStep, tools.Decide, tools.Shape, agent.OnTurnStopping and the two subagent events.

The Codex bridge becomes the codex dialect of the same x/hooks component: its own file reader, snake_case payloads without a trailing newline and always-regular-expression matchers. It shares every listener with the other dialect, so it gains the subagent points it lacked.

The bundle exists to mount the ralph tool beside a workflow engine isolated for it. The Go loop uses no workflow engine, so the bundle reduces to the x.ralph component's default-off optional bundle entry.

The OAR runtime bridge is kept by owner decision. x/oar registers one Runner per configured instance on area A12's subagent seam and drives the operator-installed OAR as a bridge child the host owns, as the library specification sets out; nothing of OAR is embedded or patched.

The bundle mounts a private terminal registry with the panel backend and the tools. The Go design has one terminal service in every profile (area A09), so the bundle reduces to the x.termtools component's default-off optional bundle entry.

Its backend made agent terminals into sidebar terminals so a person could watch them. In Go a browser already attaches to area A09's one terminal service, so no second backend is built. What remains is the control rule (the first typed input passes control to the person, with no hand-back), specified here, and the two user-terminal read tools, which move into x/termtools and are off by default.

The ralph tool is kept as x/ralph. The fixed JavaScript workflow script becomes a Go loop that calls the subagent runtime once per round; the human-turn rule and the recursion ban are enforced by a guard, and time and token budgets and one retry of a failed round are added.

The selector tool maps model-visible aliases to provider instances and nothing else. Area A12's delegation tool already accepts operator-declared targets (alias, provider, description), so subagent_oar is a mount of that tool with a target list and no package of its own.

The six terminal tools are kept as x/termtools: thin declarations over area A09's terminal.Service with the calling agent as owner. They gain named keys and full-screen reads, and report who controls each terminal.

The runtime is kept as x/webhook: it matches a verified delivery against rules and creates an ordinary root session in upstream's order with rollback before the prompt is admitted. Rules become configuration or a host-owned command instead of in-process callbacks, and a delivery record removes duplicate sessions.

The GitHub adapter is kept as x/webhook/github with upstream's check order and status codes: method, content type, bounded body, three headers, secret, signature over the raw bytes, then parsing and 202. The signature check is standard-library code and the route is the only mount of a listener separate from the UI.
Auto review stays a default-off optional bundle that no default profile, general setting or new-session default selects; the user must enable the component and then choose the preset for one session.
justification: The reviewer is a fallible model that lets calls run with full access, so making it reachable without an explicit choice would widen every installation. The interaction area also keeps the rule that auto cannot be a default preset.

reason: The mods bridge that could submit text with user authority is not built. In the Go design hook context carries source kind hook and a webhook prompt source kind webhook, and neither counts as instruction for the reviewer; only a carrier writes a user source. A test asserts that hook and webhook text never authorises a medium-risk action.

Narrowed. There is no run_code transport: a script is the argument of a shell tool call, which is reviewed, and every nested call the script makes through the tool command line is reviewed too. What remains is that auto still executes with the full-access sandbox, and that what a script does directly is judged from its visible text only.
justification: The preset's meaning is full access gated by review, as upstream decided; a script is an ordinary process whose direct effects are not tool calls (DH-ADR-8), so no per-effect review point exists.

reason: The reviewer can still misclassify, and the design adds no tool exemptions, configurable policy or retry of a verdict. Two deterministic layers exist around it: deny-only guards still run after an allow, and under the ask policy a denial reaches a person, whose session grant then applies by scope.
justification: A model classifier is not a deterministic boundary and exemptions or a configurable policy would lower the fixed ceiling upstream chose on purpose. The limit is stated to the user when the preset is selected.

reason: An in-process child that inherits auto reviews its own calls. A child run by an external provider (Claude Code, Codex, an OAR runtime) keeps that product's permission system once the parent's delegation call was allowed.
justification: The harness cannot place a reviewer inside another vendor's agent; external products run in an operator-fixed mode by the subagent area's decision, and the delegation call itself is reviewed.

reason: The Go session contract has no synchronous snapshot reader. The reviewer request is an auxiliary request built by a registered pure builder from one committed event (autoreview/requested) and the log at that position, so the request is a function of the log and can be rebuilt and compared in a test.

The limit lists which drawing surfaces and input events of the mod interface the bridge serves. The bridge runs JavaScript modules inside the host and is not built, so there is no drawing surface to complete.

The limit says the bridge does not read a mod's plugin.json and hooks.json. No mod loader exists in the Go design; a settings hook file is read by the hooks component when the operator lists it as a source.

The limit describes how the JavaScript middleware chain treats a second call to next. There is no in-process middleware chain for third-party code in Go: a hook is a separate process that returns one answer.
The limit lists mod event names the bridge registers but never raises. The mod event interface is not built; the lifecycle points the Go design offers are the nine hook points of the specification.
The limit lists members of the $ host object the bridge does not serve. The $ object is a JavaScript interface handed to code running in the host, which the Go design does not have.

The limit says a mod's tool.call handler runs after the permission decision and cannot rewrite arguments. The handler is not built. For hooks the order is stated instead: a pre-tool hook runs at the policy stage, before guards and approval, and can never rewrite logged arguments.

The limit is that module-level variables and environment writes of a mod are shared by every session because the module is loaded once into one Node process. No module is loaded into the Go host; a hook is a fresh process per event with no shared memory.

The limit is that a mod runs in the host process with Node's globals and full authority, with no sandbox, static check or hot reload. It exists only because JavaScript is loaded into the host, which the Go design never does.
The limit concerns where the text returned by a mod's turn.complete handler is shown. The handler is not built. A hook's systemMessage is recorded on hook/result and shown as a transcript notice.
The limit lists fields of $.session.usage and $.fs.stat that the bridge reports as zero or empty. Both are members of the JavaScript host interface that is not built.
The limit lists what the React band component cannot draw (panes, text input, hotkeys, sizing props). The band is a client component for mods and is not built.
The limit is that the band redraws only on the bridge's redraw triggers. There is no band and no bridge in the Go design.

A hook's updatedInput is still never honoured. In Go it is not even representable: the hook Output type has no field for replacement arguments and the pipeline's decision types carry none. A test checks that logged arguments are byte-identical after a hook returned updatedInput.
justification: Outcome DH-O-6 requires that logged arguments are never rewritten, and the tools area dropped the input-rewrite proposal. A hook that wants a different call denies with a message and the model retries.

reason: The run-level halt exists in Go: a hook answer with continue false makes the component cancel the open turn through the agent's Cancel with cause extension, inbox kept, and the hook's stopReason as the recorded reason on turn/end.
Only command hooks run, now also in the argument-list form. http, mcp_tool, prompt and agent handlers are listed in the sources diagnostics and skipped.
justification: An http handler would send event data off the machine without an opt-in (DH-ADR-9), and prompt and agent handlers are model calls outside the session log. They are deliberately not offered by decision DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1.

reason: Narrowed from 23 unsupported events to 21: SessionEnd and PostToolUseFailure are added. The other events are not offered; an entry for one is kept in the sources diagnostics list instead of being silently ignored.
justification: Each remaining event needs a seam another area owns or has no counterpart in this product (worktrees, teammates, elicitation). The component is a compatibility adapter for a third-party contract that keeps growing, not a reimplementation of Claude Code.

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: the hook is awaited through the ordered agent.Created event, so its context is in the first request; plain standard output is accepted as context; the payload carries the model. Still not offered: initialUserMessage, sessionTitle, watchPaths, reloadSkills and CLAUDE_ENV_FILE.
justification: The remaining fields let a hook start a turn, rename a session or change the environment of later commands, which are outside the closed set of answers a hook may give (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1).

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: plain standard output is accepted as context and the default timeout for this point is 30 seconds. Still not offered: sessionTitle and suppressOriginalPrompt.
justification: Hiding or replacing the user's prompt would be a rewrite of what the person typed; a hook may reject a prompt or add context after it, nothing else (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1).

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: additionalContext from a pre-tool hook is delivered with the same call's result. Kept: allow never pre-approves, defer is not offered and updatedInput is never honoured.
justification: A hook's answer can only restrict: letting an external program return allow would skip the policy listeners, guards and approval behind it, and a rewrite would break the rule that logged arguments stay as written (DH-O-6).

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: tool_response carries the rendered text and the structured value. Kept: updatedToolOutput and updatedMCPToolOutput are not offered; a post-tool hook may block with feedback or add context.
justification: Replacing a tool's content or value from an external program is outside the closed answers of DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1; the result the model sees stays the tool's own or a logged block.

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: the payload names the real provider as agent_type and reports the creator's session with the child as agent_id, and the stop payload carries the bounded last answer from the settled record. Kept: start context reaches a local child only, and the stop hook only observes.
justification: An external child is another vendor's process with no inbox to inject into, and a child's result is settled by the subagent area's lifecycle, which a hook must not block.

reason: The Stop point is completed: stop_hook_active is true after the first forced continuation of a turn, last_assistant_message is filled from the log, background_tasks and session_crons are filled from the job registry and schedule service when mounted, and forced continuations are capped by maxStopContinuations (default 3) on top of the driver's turn budget.

Narrowed. Fixed: payloads carry the turn id, the session's preset name and its model and effort; systemMessage is recorded and shown as a notice; continue false halts the turn; transcript_path is filled with an export file when the source sets transcript. Not applied: suppressOutput and terminalSequence, and transcript_path stays empty by default because the session lives in a database, not a file.
justification: The two output flags address a terminal interface this product does not have, and writing an export file for every hook run would cost a full log read per event, so it is opt-in per source.

reason: Narrowed. Fixed: the args (no shell) and shell options are honoured, matched hooks run concurrently and identical commands once, sources are a list, a project file is discovered per session behind a trust digest, and files are re-read on change. Kept: only command handlers run, and async, asyncRewake, if, once and statusMessage are not honoured.
justification: Asynchronous hooks would answer after the decision they were asked about, and the other options belong to Claude Code's own interface; the non-command handlers are excluded by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1.

reason: Narrowed from five unsupported events to three: the codex dialect shares the engine's listeners, so SubagentStart and SubagentStop fire for it too. PermissionRequest, PreCompact and PostCompact are not offered; an entry for one is listed in the sources diagnostics, not silently dropped.
justification: A permission-request hook would let an external program take part in an approval, which only an owner's answerer may settle, and the compaction points belong to another area's transaction.

reason: SessionStart hooks run on the ordered agent.Created event, which the agent area awaits before the first turn, so their context is in the first model request. A test asserts it.

Both controls are honoured at UserPromptSubmit: systemMessage is recorded on hook/result and shown as a transcript notice, and continue false rejects the prompt and cancels the turn with cause extension.

Narrowed. Fixed: tool_input is the call's full logged argument object, not only a command field, and additionalContext is delivered with the same call's result. Kept: permissionDecision allow pre-approves nothing and updatedInput is never honoured.
justification: A hook's answer can only restrict (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1) and logged arguments are never rewritten (DH-O-6).

reason: The PostToolUse payload carries the full logged arguments and a structured tool_response (rendered text plus the typed value), and continue false cancels the turn with cause extension.

The Stop payload reports the real stop_hook_active and last_assistant_message, continue false halts the turn, and consecutive forced continuations are capped by maxStopContinuations, so an unconditionally blocking hook can no longer loop for ever.

Payload values come from the live session: the model actually selected and the session's permission preset name replace the static configured model and the constant default. systemMessage is shown, continue false is applied, and transcript_path is filled with an export file when the source asks for one, which removes the cause (no artifact path was reachable).

Narrowed. Fixed: several sources may be listed, a project file is discovered per session behind a trust digest, and matched hooks run concurrently. Kept: only synchronous command handlers run, Codex's inline config.toml hook form is not read, and statusMessage and commandWindows are ignored.
justification: The harness reads the JSON hook file both products share and does not add a TOML reader for one field of another product's configuration; asynchronous hooks cannot answer the decision they were asked about.

reason: The need for explicit human intent is enforced, not only stated in the prompt: a guard denies ralph unless the open turn is a human turn and the caller is not a delegated agent. Token cost is bounded by round, time and token budgets. The loop is Go code that calls the subagent runtime, so no workflow engine is mounted or isolated for it.

Runtime coverage is unchanged: the real-environment scenario runs one installed runtime, and the five runtimes upstream never verified (antigravity, grok, kimi, opencode, pi) have a path through the bridge that nobody has shown to work.
justification: Verifying a runtime needs that vendor's program and an account; the design gives every registered runtime the same host-owned bridge and states which were verified with which OAR version.

reason: The provider still installs, signs in and upgrades nothing. Narrowed: what is missing (Node, the OAR package, the native agent, a version outside the range) is reported by the provider's requirements list and as subagent/unavailable before any task text is sent, and never fails host start-up.
justification: External agent runtimes are operator-installed programs by owner decision DH-ADR-23; the harness downloads and bundles nothing.

reason: Native permission modes still apply with no harness approval prompt. Narrowed: an instance loads only with a stated permission posture or the literal bypass setting, an approval or input request that OAR reports ends the run instead of waiting, and every instance has a time limit.
justification: OAR offers no channel through which a person could answer the native agent, so the provider declares that it cannot ask and fails closed on a request.

reason: The host owns the bridge child and every process below it, so cancelling while the native session opens stops the process tree at once instead of waiting for OAR, and the time limit covers start-up as well as the turn.

Narrowed. Fixed: the bridge child is started through the one process starter and owned by the run, so cancel, time limit, a failed start and disposal end the whole tree before the result is reported. Kept: the native agent applies its own mode instead of the harness sandbox (the settled record says confined by-product), and it may keep transcripts of its own.
justification: A native agent needs the network and its own sign-in files, which no harness sandbox policy grants today, and its history belongs to the user's installation of that product.

reason: Narrowed. A structured answer can be requested because the subagent manager validates an output schema for every provider, and unlogged activity can be shown through the seam's progress event. Kept: one task, one native session, with no follow-up, no resume and no rollback of files the agent changed.
justification: The bridge drives OAR exactly as upstream does (one prompt, wait for the turn to end); continuation across OAR sessions is not something the upstream checkout shows to be possible, and file changes by another vendor's agent cannot be undone by the harness.

reason: There is one terminal service, provided by the execution area in every profile, so the terminal tools need no web composition and no private registry; in a headless profile they work without the roster view.

This bullet only points at the sidebar backend's list of limits. That backend is not a separate component in Go, and each of its six limits has its own row (terminal-panel.1 to .6) with its own disposition.
After a person typed into an agent terminal the agent cannot regain input; it reads the terminal and opens a new one.
justification: Once a person has typed, the shell may hold a sudo or ssh sign-in; handing input back would give the model that authority with no approval. Upstream rejected a shared terminal for the same reason.

reason: A command typed into an agent terminal runs under the policy the shell was started with and cannot request more access; the guidance sends a denied command to the one-shot shell tool, which can ask.
justification: An approval covers one call, and a persistent shell has one launch plan for its whole life; widening a running shell would turn one approval into a standing one.

reason: Readiness after terminal_send is still inferred where it cannot be proven. Narrowed by the execution area's readiness tiers: the shell at its prompt is exact on Linux and macOS through the prompt marker, a program waiting for terminal input is provable on Linux only, and silence is reported as inferred_idle with the reason in the result.
justification: A terminal never says done; only the operating system can show that a foreign program is blocked reading the terminal, and macOS and Windows do not expose it.

reason: user_terminal_read returns the screen as it is and never waits for new output.
justification: The model has read access to a person's terminal, not a claim on it: a waiting read would tie a tool call to the person's own work and keep reading what they type next. The model reads again when it needs to.

reason: Agent terminals use the execution area's one shell backend with its controlled bootstrap, which runs no user start-up files, so no start-up file can fail to write outside the write roots. The cost is stated: a person who takes the terminal over gets a bare shell. This depends on area A09 confirming the default start arguments.

terminal_open starts every agent shell with history disabled (no history file for bash, history saving off for PowerShell) in every sandbox mode, so the agent's commands never join the person's history and the agent's shell never loads it. A real-environment scenario checks the history file is unchanged.
Completion is still the worker's own claim; no evaluator ships. The result labels the status as worker-reported and names which bound ended the run.
justification: An evaluator needs its own inputs, tools, checks and authority, which upstream left undefined and which the goals area also carries. Adding one here would be a new feature, not a port.

reason: A ralph run is foreground only: the tool call blocks until the run settles, with no job id, resume checkpoint or scheduler.
justification: The run is authorised by the human turn it was asked in; a background loop would outlive that turn and spend tokens with nobody watching. A person who wants background delegation uses a workflow job.

reason: The workspace and one bounded report are still the only memory across rounds.
justification: A fresh context per round is the purpose of the tool; carrying conversation across rounds would make it a goal, which another area owns.

reason: One round is still one fresh child from one operator-chosen provider, with no fan-out inside a round and no provider chosen by the model.
justification: Fan-out and routing are what workflows and the delegation tool are for; keeping the loop fixed is what lets the model supply data only.

reason: Recursion is denied structurally: a guard refuses ralph when the calling agent is a delegated agent, so a round's child cannot start a loop of its own whatever the prompt says. A test asserts it.

A failed round is retried roundRetries times (default 1) with the same handoff before the run ends, and because the loop is Go code and not a script in an engine, the failed round number and the last good report are always returned.
A run is bounded by rounds, by maxDuration and by maxTokens counted from each round's reported usage; the result names the bound that ended it.

Targets of the selector are one-shot: no follow-up or resume, and no per-call override of native permissions. Narrowed: a structured answer can be requested through the shared delegation tool's output schema.
justification: The provider declares that it is not continuable, and the permission mode is fixed by the operator so that a model cannot widen another vendor's agent.

reason: The selector is area A12's delegation tool, whose visibility is resolved per step from the registered providers, and a provider with a missing prerequisite says so in its requirements list. A call to an unavailable target fails as subagent/unavailable before any task text is sent.

Behaviour no longer varies by provider: every external provider uses the subagent area's one run lifecycle for start, cancel, cleanup and settlement. Ownership is explicit: an accepted run belongs to the root's tree fiber, so removing a tool is not expected to revoke it, and the creator can interrupt or dismiss it.

terminal_send accepts named keys (for example escape, arrow keys, ctrl-c) and terminal_read returns the emulated screen including a full-screen program's alternate screen, so a terminal interface can be driven and read. The bell and declarative auto-start remain carried by the execution area's own rows.
The run_in_background field is part of the terminal_send schema only while the job registry and the job tools are in the step view, so the model is never offered an argument that is then rejected.

The ingress is a second instance of the host area's listener, which supports TLS and refuses a non-loopback address without it, so the ingress can terminate TLS itself. This depends on area A18 allowing a second listener instance.

Field checks are part of the rule engine: a declarative rule's conditions read payload fields by pointer, a missing or wrongly typed field makes the condition false, and a field named in include that is absent fails the rule, so a rule cannot consume a field it did not check.

202 is still answered before rules run and before any session exists, so the provider learns nothing about downstream work. Narrowed: the delivery record, keyed by the provider's delivery id, names the sessions created or the failure category.
justification: The wire decision DH-ADR-WIRE-12 keeps the runtime fire-and-forget: holding the provider's request open for rule and session work would tie an internet-facing connection to model activity.

reason: Only application/json bodies are accepted; a form-encoded delivery is answered 415.
justification: GitHub lets the operator choose JSON, and one content type keeps the handler's input surface to one decoder that runs only after the signature was verified.

reason: The runtime still has no queue and replays nothing by itself. Narrowed: a delivery is recorded before 202, a crash leaves its record in the received state, and a redelivery of a received or failed record runs the rules again.
justification: DH-ADR-WIRE-12 keeps the runtime fire-and-forget; the provider's own redelivery is the retry, and an automatic replay could start unattended work the operator no longer wants.

reason: A machine-state table keyed by source and delivery id records each delivery for dedupWindow (default 72 hours). A redelivery whose record is admitted or no-match runs no rule and creates no session.
Acceptance and rule settlement still report nothing about the agent's success or output. Narrowed: the delivery record names the session ids, so an operator can open the session and see its state.
justification: After the prompt is admitted the session is an ordinary one that the runtime no longer owns; a completion report would need the runtime to watch sessions, which upstream and the wire decision deliberately avoid.

reason: A rule is configuration that the host evaluates itself, or a command run as a child process through the hook runner. The host stops that process tree with the stop ladder on unload or timeout, so no rule code can ignore cancellation.
The runtime never creates a workspace: a rule must name a workspace that is already registered, checked when the session is requested, so a failed session attempt leaves no workspace behind.
The TODO asks for a run-level halt for a hook's continue false. The Go component cancels the open turn through the agent's Cancel with cause extension and records the hook's stopReason.

The TODO asks for a cap on consecutive forced continuations. maxStopContinuations (default 3) counts them per turn; past the cap Stop hooks are not asked, and the driver's turn budget bounds the turn in any case.

The TODO asks for per-session discovery of a project-local hook file. With discoverProject the component looks in each session's workspace and runs the file only after an owner approved its exact content by digest.
The same TODO as in the Claude Code bridge: continue false needs a run-level halt. Both dialects share the listener that cancels the turn with cause extension.
The TODO notes that Codex supplies stop_hook_active so a Stop hook can limit itself. The payload now reports the real value, and the component caps forced continuations itself.
The TODO asks for per-session project-local discovery of the Codex hook file. Project discovery is dialect-independent and gated by the same trust digest.

The Go harness exposes no separate tool definition: subagent_oar is area A12's delegation tool mounted under that name with operator-declared targets, each mapping an alias to an OAR provider instance. The model still picks an alias and cannot change launch arguments.
The same read-only tool, over the user-terminal service of area A19. Changed: it is registered only when readUserTerminals is set, which is off by default, and it is hidden from delegated agents.

The same read-only tool: it returns the newest screen lines of one of the person's terminals, bounded, and never waits or writes. Changed: off by default, because that text is logged and sent to the model provider.

The Go harness exposes ralph with the same two arguments, objective and maxRounds, and the same three terminal statuses. Changed: the call is denied outside a human turn and for a delegated agent, and the result names the bound (rounds, time or tokens) that ended the run.
The same tool with the same argument. It ends the shell and waits for its process tree, or reports released when a person has taken control and the shell must keep running.
The same tool: it lists the calling agent's own sessions. Changed: each entry also reports who controls the terminal.
The same tool with type, name and cwd. Changed: the shell is the execution area's one backend, started with history disabled, and the start-up output is the emulated screen.
The same tool with sessionId, offset and count. Changed: it reads the host-side emulated screen and scrollback, so a full-screen program is readable.

The same tool with sessionId, text, submit and run_in_background. Changed: a keys argument sends named keys, the wait reason is the execution area's, the background field appears only with the job tools, and a send fails with an explanation once a person controls the terminal.

The same tool with sessionId and signal. A signal the platform cannot deliver to the foreground group is refused with a stated reason, never ignored, and a signal is refused once a person controls the terminal.

The bridge's settings (hook and process timeouts, band size, tool aliases) configure a component that is not built. The one idea kept is the alias table from Claude Code tool names to harness tool names, which becomes hooks.Config.toolAliases.

Replaced by the Go struct oar.Config: name, runtime, node, package, model, effort, launchArgs, allowPermissionBypass, env, maxDuration and stopGrace. Changed: a permission posture must be stated or the instance does not load, and the time limit is required instead of optional.
Its two fields, the alias-to-provider map and the tool name, are the targets list and tool field of area A12's delegation tool configuration; no struct of its own exists.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep, with two changes. The fixed three-level policy, one review per call with no exemptions, authority from recorded sources and a denial that never runs the body are ported as a tools.Decide listener. Changed: the note keeps reviewer prompts and decisions outside the log, and the Go design logs the request event and the verdict so the review can be rebuilt; and unloading the component moves live auto sessions to read-only, not to full access as the note specifies. The first verdict's remark on program effects is recorded as carried unit auto-review.3.

Final verdict: keep. Under the ask policy a reviewer denial returns the pipeline's Ask decision after later listeners allowed the call, so a person can overrule it; under never it is a final denial with its own code; a reviewer failure is a failure with a distinct code and is never asked. This maps directly onto the closed decisions of the tools area.

Final verdict: keep the rule, drop the mechanism. Ownership by creator, takeover on the first typed input, reads that continue, no escalation inside and read-only access to the person's terminals are kept. The separate backend is not built because the execution area's one terminal service is already what a browser attaches to. Two changes: reading the person's terminals is off by default, and subagents are not refused. The note's rejection of the sandbox-mode fence conflicts with the execution area's kept fence and is raised as an open question.

Final verdict: keep. Text whose recorded source is the user is instruction whether a person or a supervising program sent it, and files, tool results, hook context and webhook prompts never are. An explicit never policy gives unattended runs a structured final denial. The Go design relies on the same rule to keep hook and webhook text from authorising anything.

Final verdict confirmed after reading the note: it removes one array copy and one deep-freeze pass in the JavaScript reviewer. Go has no freeze step, and the Go reviewer request is built by a pure function over the committed log, so there is no intermediate snapshot to copy or borrow.
